items.title: Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back
items.content_text:
Three Exchanges, Three States, One Week: The Industry Sued Back

For months, the courtroom traffic ran one way: states sued prediction markets. In the last week of October, the exchanges flipped the script. Between October 26 and 27, Nadex, Kalshi and Polymarket US each walked into a different federal court and sued a state of their own.

Polymarket US moved in Louisiana. Its operator, QCX LLC, sued Attorney General Liz Murrill and the Gaming Control Board on October 27 in the Eastern District of Louisiana, case No. 2:26-cv-02482, arguing the Commodity Exchange Act preempts state enforcement and that the state's stance violates the Commerce Clause. The complaint points to a December 5, 2025 advisory calling sports event contracts illegal gambling, and notes the state's 20 sports wagering licenses go first to in-state casino and racetrack licensees.

Kalshi took Missouri the same day. KalshiEX LLC sued Attorney General Catherine Hanaway and the Gaming Commission in the Eastern District of Missouri, case No. 4:26-cv-01860, on a single claim: federal preemption under the Supremacy Clause. Missouri's September 16 cease-and-desist called Kalshi an unlicensed sports wagering platform and gave it 14 extra days to comply; Kalshi will seek a preliminary injunction, and a restraining order if the state will not stand down.

The third front is Utah, where North American Derivatives Exchange, trading as OG.com Prediction Markets, sued Attorney General Derek Brown on October 26 in the District of Utah, case No. 2:26-cv-01056, before Judge David Barlow. A CFTC-designated contract market since 2004, Nadex launched OG.com in February 2026 and raises express, field and conflict preemption. The same week, the United States and the CFTC sued Utah themselves, days after Utah sued Kalshi on October 20, and Kalshi separately sued Louisiana officials on October 23. The CFTC is now battling 10 states in court.

One federal rulebook or fifty state ones is no longer a panel argument. It is being litigated simultaneously by the regulator and by three competing exchanges that agree on almost nothing else.

Sources: RG, CoinDesk

items.content_text:
The Model and the Market Agree to the Point

Saturday's two biggest college football games come with a rare sight: the trading market and the simulation model are pricing them almost identically. On Kalshi, Georgia is an 80-cent favorite over Florida, with Florida at 21 cents, ahead of their 3:30 p.m. ET kickoff. SportsLine's projection model, which simulates the game 10,000 times, has Georgia winning 81% of the time — one point from the market.

The primetime game is the same story. Ohio State is priced at 69 cents on Kalshi for its trip to USC, with USC at 32 cents. The same simulation model puts Ohio State's win rate at 70%. Two venues of judgment — thousands of traders putting money down, and a model running ten thousand simulated Saturdays — landed within a single point of each other, twice in one day.

Where the certainty ends is the margin. Earlier on the slate, Notre Dame was priced near 97% to beat Navy on roughly $2.9 million of volume, yet the market gave Notre Dame only a 51% chance of winning by more than 30.5 points, and just 47% for the game to clear 55.5 total points. Miami's spread against North Carolina tells the same story, with Miami to cover 14.5 priced at 49 cents — a genuine coin flip.

That split is what makes a Saturday board worth reading. The moneyline answers who wins, and on the biggest games it now matches the computers almost exactly. The spread and total markets answer how it happens, and there the market is honestly undecided — priced at 49, 51 and 47 cents, where a single drive moves the number.

Sources: SportsLine, SportsBettingDime, Action Network

items.title: The Lab Now Has a Ticker: Drug Trials Became a Trade
items.content_text:
The Lab Now Has a Ticker: Drug Trials Became a Trade

Prediction markets have left the election and the stadium and entered the laboratory. Polymarket has hosted biotech contracts since May, and on July 16 Kalshi launched a suite of markets on Phase 3 trial outcomes and full FDA approvals. Volume topped $100,000 shortly after launch across about 13 markets tied to companies including Sanofi, Eli Lilly and Gilead Sciences.

The board is still live and specific. As of October 30, Kalshi offered odds on when the FDA will approve Eli Lilly's retatrutide, while Polymarket offered odds on by what date the FDA will approve Moderna's melanoma vaccine, intismeran autogene. Pharmaceutical Technology reports users may place hundreds of thousands of dollars on outcomes like these.

The stakes explain the interest. Bringing a single drug to market costs an estimated $2.3 billion, and as of the FDA's April 2026 figures, roughly 30 percent of trials required to report results had posted none. Kalshi, working with AppliedXL, says a public contract can produce a continuously updated public probability, and it framed the markets in May as a way to help solve drug development's information silo problem.

The guardrails are part of the story. Kalshi's pilot covers only late-stage trials, lists a contract only after a trial finishes enrolling, and requires employment verification for traders in these markets. Fenwick partners Chelsea Anderson and Noah Solowiejczyk told Pharmaceutical Technology the markets are here to stay, but that private biotechs, once shielded from this exposure, now face a new insider-trading risk and likely more regulation.

Sources: Pharmaceutical Technology, Yogonet, CryptoBriefing

items.title: Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer
items.content_text:
Prices Get Smarter as Deadlines Get Closer

Prediction markets are often judged on their worst screenshot: a stale price from a thin market, quoted months early. Kalshi's August 2026 accuracy study measured the whole curve instead, and found its predictions generally became more accurate as events approached, especially in markets with more traders and more trading activity.

An independent check across nine resolved markets in politics, sports and pop culture found the same shape. An 80-cent contract that loses is not automatically a bad forecast; the other outcome carried a real 20% chance, and across many similar markets those chances are the product being sold.

The two levers in the study are the ones traders can actually see before they buy: time to resolution and crowd size. A liquid market near its deadline is a measurement. A thin market far from one is a rumor with a price tag.

Read that way, the industry's growth is itself an accuracy story. Record crowds and record volume do not just make exchanges richer. They make every number on the board harder to fool.

Same Senate Question, Two Different Answers

Ask two exchanges who wins the Senate and you get two different races. Kalshi prices Democratic Senate control at 71 cents, and its balance-of-power contract puts a Democratic sweep at 70 cents. On Polymarket US, the same Senate question trades at 47%.

A 24-point gap on the cycle's biggest question is not a rounding error. The venues run different books with different crowds: Kalshi's midterm complex counts 311 tradeable contracts and tens of millions in open interest, while the Polymarket US Senate market traded just $77K in the last 24 hours.

Thin books price noisily. A $77K day can be moved by a handful of orders, while Kalshi's price is set by a crowd that has been building positions for months. When two prices disagree this much, the deeper market is usually the one quoting information; the thinner one is quoting whoever showed up today.

Election night will grade both. Until then, the gap itself is the data point: it measures how much of the prediction-market map is deep water and how much is still a puddle.

items.title: Award Shows Gave Prediction Markets Their Receipts
items.content_text:
Award Shows Gave Prediction Markets Their Receipts

Culture critics used to argue from taste. Increasingly they check a price first, because award season is where prediction markets built their public track record. More than $200 million traded through award contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket around the 2026 Academy Awards, and final prices called the winner in 19 of 24 categories.

The honest footnote matters as much as the headline. Most Oscar categories are effectively settled by guild awards weeks earlier, so calling them is arithmetic more than prophecy. The markets missed in several categories where the argument was genuinely live, which is exactly where an oracle earns its reputation.

Kalshi's own August 2026 research adds the mechanism: its prices generally grew more accurate as events approached, especially in markets with more traders and more activity.

That is the mature version of the claim. A prediction price is a good instrument and an imperfect oracle, sharpest when the crowd is large and the deadline is near. Award season proved both halves of that sentence in public.

Cricket's fit with event contracts is structural. A match runs for hours, momentum swings by the over, and every swing is a chance to enter, exit or reverse a position. Sports that unfold slowly give exchanges something football's three-hour sprint cannot: time for a real market to form.

items.title: Sundays Trade Double Mondays: The Weekend Effect
items.content_text:
Sundays Trade Double Mondays: The Weekend Effect

Prediction markets keep office hours, just not the ones you would expect. Across the last seven whole weeks, the average Sunday traded $5.2 billion against the average Monday's $2.4 billion. The market's biggest day is the one when its traders are off work.

The busiest single day of the last 60 was Sunday, October 25, at $7.14 billion across venues. Saturdays average $4.6 billion, Fridays $3.2 billion, and the midweek days cluster under $3 billion.

Football is the obvious engine: weekends stack NFL and college slates on top of the always-on crypto windows, and parlays counted outside the category rankings added $243 million in dollars paid in the last 24 hours alone.

The strategic read is simple. Liquidity in this industry is a weekend product. Any exchange planning a launch, a new market or a headline partnership should aim it at Saturday morning, when the crowd is already there.

Seventeen Points Gone: Florida's Governor Race Slipped

Favorites are supposed to harden as Election Day approaches. Florida's governor market did the opposite. Byron Donalds has fallen from 83% to 66% over seven days on Kalshi, the largest weekly decline on the politics board.

The market still did $559K in the last 24 hours, trading at 2.2 times its daily average, so this is not a favorite quietly drifting on no volume. Money is arriving specifically to sell the favorite down, with David Jolly now at 36% on the other side.

A 17-point slide in the final week does not mean the favorite loses. At 66%, Donalds still wins two times out of three in the market's read. It means the certainty premium is gone, and every new poll or headline between now and Tuesday lands on a price with no cushion left.

Florida was supposed to be a race traders checked once and forgot. Instead it became one of the last live questions of the cycle, priced accordingly.

items.title: 477,850 Traders: Polymarket's Crowd Is the Story
items.content_text:
477,850 Traders: Polymarket's Crowd Is the Story

Volume records get the headlines, but headcount is the harder number to fake. Polymarket's monthly active traders hit an all-time high of 477,850 in October, up 93.7% from September's 246,610 and past the previous peak of 462,600 set in January.

The platform listed 38,270 new markets in the month, nearly three times August's count, and monthly volume rebounded to $3.02 billion after months below $1 billion between February and August.

Breadth matters because prediction prices are only as good as the crowd behind them. A market with twelve traders is an opinion. A market with half a million monthly participants is a measurement instrument, and October is the month that instrument got measurably bigger.

Kalshi still owns the volume crown by a wide margin. But the trader record says the audience is not consolidating onto one exchange. It is growing on both sides of the rivalry at once.

Sources: Startup Fortune, The Block

items.title: The NBA Just Picked Its Prediction Markets
items.content_text:
The NBA Just Picked Its Prediction Markets

The last major North American league without a formal position on prediction markets now has one. The NBA has named Kalshi and Polymarket its Preferred Prediction Market Exchanges, with official data from Sportradar, rights to league intellectual property, and a memorandum of understanding with the CFTC.

The league's price for legitimacy is control. The agreements limit which NBA markets the exchanges may offer, ban league and team personnel from trading NBA contracts, and require suspicious trading to be reported and shared for investigations. DraftKings was elevated to an Authorized Prediction Market Operator under the same framework.

The NBA joins MLB and the NHL in signing information-sharing arrangements with the regulator, a pattern that is quietly becoming the industry's operating template: official data in, integrity data out.

Five days ago these exchanges were counterparties the league had no deals with. Now they settle NBA markets on the league's own data feed. That is what mainstream looks like when it arrives.

Sources: NBC Sports, RotoWire, Cointelegraph

items.title: A Billion Dollars Says This Is a Financial Market Now
items.content_text:
A Billion Dollars Says This Is a Financial Market Now

Kalshi has raised $1 billion in a Series G round co-led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital, at a $40 billion valuation. Rounds this size are not about survival. They are about what the company says it is becoming.

The numbers in the announcement point past event contracts. Non-sports revenue has passed $1 billion annualized. Perpetual futures have traded $83 billion with more than 500,000 traders since launching a few months ago. Commodities fees passed $100 million annualized within three months. More than 30 million accounts exist, and annualized volume across the business exceeds $1 trillion.

The roadmap is just as telling: indices built with S and P, single-stock perpetual futures, and compute markets, plus expansion across Latin America and Europe.

Prediction markets began as a way to price elections. A $40 billion valuation says investors now price them as financial infrastructure that happens to list elections too.

Sources: Croupier, Coin Edition

items.title: The Weekend Clock: What to Watch After the Binance Hack
items.content_text:
The Weekend Clock: What to Watch After the Binance Hack

The Binance story now runs on three clocks, and all of them strike within days. First: withdrawals. In their October 30 letter, co-CEOs Yi He and Richard Teng targeted a phased resumption of withdrawals within about 34 hours, once security checks are complete — a window that points at Sunday, November 1. Binance stresses the restart will be phased, not simultaneous for every asset or account, and the exchange has not yet confirmed that withdrawals have resumed.

Second: proof of reserves. Binance planned an initial reserves snapshot within 12 hours of its update, with results due Monday, November 2. Those results have not been published yet. When they land, they are the first hard check on Binance's pledge that its $6.34 billion set-aside fully covers the theft.

Third: the coins that cannot be frozen. About $3.3 billion of the stolen assets sit outside issuer control, including 18,270 BTC split across 19 wallets, per Elliptic figures reported by Cointribune. Any move from those wallets toward an exchange is the market's clearest sell-pressure signal; Compass Point analysts are watching bitcoin's $75,000 to $77,000 range in the meantime.

Also due: Binance's fuller technical findings, expected within about 48 hours of its update, and a promised post-mortem. Until those land, the hack's final shape — how the attackers got in, and what changes because of it — is still being written.

Sources: Binance update via Forbes, CryptoBriefing, CoinDesk, Cointribune

items.title: Bitcoin Fell 4 Percent on the Biggest Hack in History
items.content_text:
Bitcoin Fell 4 Percent on the Biggest Hack in History

A $6.3 billion theft at the world's largest exchange knocked bitcoin down about 4 percent. In 2018, a failed attack on the same exchange — one that stole nothing — knocked it down roughly 11 percent. The difference between those two numbers is the story of how this market has changed.

Bitcoin tumbled to a six-week low of $76,368 as the news broke, then pared losses to trade near $77,300 on Friday and about $77,509 on Saturday morning, per Finnhub. Ether fell to $2,178, a two-month low, before recovering toward $2,246. Leveraged traders took the sharpest hit: about $1.5 billion in liquidations, $468 million of it in bitcoin and $358 million in ether, according to Cryptowisser.

Crypto stocks fell harder than crypto. Coinbase closed down 10.6% on October 30, Strategy fell 7.8% and Robinhood 7.2%, per DefiLlama equity data cited by Coinjuice — a reminder that the equity wrappers carry exchange risk even when the networks themselves were never breached.

Analysts split on what comes next. Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan expects bitcoin's price to recover within a week, and TD Cowen, Cantor Fitzgerald and Compass Point all called the selloff a buying opportunity. Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick is the caution, expecting pressure until the frozen assets' status clears. With a crypto market worth about $2.6 trillion and U.S. spot ETFs holding roughly 1.3 million BTC, the shock absorbers are simply bigger than in 2018.

Sources: WSJ, Cointribune, Cryptowisser, Finnhub

items.title: Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be.
items.content_text:
Half the Loot Is Frozen. The Other Half Cannot Be.

The fastest number in the Binance story is not the $6.3 billion stolen. It is the roughly $3 billion frozen within hours, as the industry's biggest issuers moved in coordination: Tether froze more than $1.567 billion in USDT, Circle froze more than $800 million in USDC, and Ripple and World Liberty Financial blocked additional tokens, according to CoinDesk.

The catch is structural. Stablecoins can be frozen because an issuer controls them. Bitcoin cannot — there is no issuer to call. Arkham data cited by CoinDesk shows the attacker has already split about $1.4 billion in stolen bitcoin — 18,270 BTC — across 19 wallets, and has borrowed 20,000 wrapped ether, roughly $44 million, through Aave using stolen USDT as collateral.

Freezing is also not the same as recovery. Legal experts told CoinDesk that blocked tokens are stopped, not returned; getting them back to Binance is a separate legal process. The speed of this freeze has raised an uncomfortable question inside the industry: smaller hack victims usually wait on court orders, while the largest exchange in the world got a $3 billion freeze in hours.

That asymmetry is now part of the security debate. The breach entered through a laptop and internal systems, not stolen keys — which means the next round of exchange safeguards will be about endpoints, approvals and withdrawal controls, not just wallet architecture.

Sources: CoinDesk, Arkham

items.title: The Odds Board Priced the Hack in Hours
items.content_text:
The Odds Board Priced the Hack in Hours

Prediction markets did not wait for the post-mortem. Within hours of the Binance breach becoming public, Polymarket's weekly bitcoin line (October 26 to November 1) put a 46% chance on bitcoin trading at or below $76,000 before the week closes on Sunday, according to RG.org's market wrap. Bitcoin's overnight low near $76,400 came within about half a percent of that line without touching it.

The repricing was sharpest in the October contracts. Polymarket's "Bitcoin dips to $75,000 in October" market jumped from 5% to 20% as the hack landed, one of the biggest 24-hour movers on the board. Traders were pricing a second leg down, not a collapse: the recovery strikes stayed alive on the same board, and bitcoin steadied near $77,300 by Friday morning.

Kalshi's daily ladder told the same story in smaller increments. Its "What price will Bitcoin hit on October 31?" market, with $173K traded in 24 hours as observed on the morning of October 31, priced the $78,000 strike at 56%, per DeFi Rate's market data. The 15-minute up-or-down markets on both venues kept cycling through the volatility — 96 settlements a day — with Down favored in the early Saturday windows.

The board's verdict, for now: a real shock, a priced-in tail risk, and no panic premium for disaster. That changes only if the stolen coins start moving — or if withdrawals stay closed longer than promised.

Sources: RG.org, DeFi Rate, CoinDesk

items.title: Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack
items.content_text:
Twenty Minutes, $6.3 Billion: The State of the Binance Hack

At about 20:05 UTC on Thursday, October 29, attackers drained an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance's hot wallets across several blockchains. Most of the coins — bitcoin, ether and stablecoins among them — left in a burst that lasted roughly 20 minutes, according to CoinDesk. It is the largest theft in crypto history, more than four times the $1.46 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025.

Binance says the entry point was a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let the attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal requests through internal systems. The exchange says it later found additional exploit points, but has seen no evidence that any wallet private keys were stolen.

Blockchain analysts moved fast on attribution. TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group with high confidence, citing the speed and sophistication of the operation. The FBI says it is engaged with public and private partners, and the U.S. Secret Service says its investigators are working with Circle and others to trace and freeze the funds.

Two numbers now define the story. Binance has set aside more than $6.34 billion of its own resources to restore customer balances, and industry partners have frozen about $3 billion of the stolen assets. Withdrawals remain paused pending security checks; deposits remain open.

Sources: CoinDesk, CNN, TRM Labs

items.title: 96 Percent to 27: The Flip Is Complete
items.content_text:
96 Percent to 27: The Flip Is Complete

Two years ago Polymarket was the prediction market. It held about 95 percent of the market in September 2024 and 96 percent at its peak. That era is over. Its share has fallen to 27 percent, and Kalshi now trades nearly three times its volume.

October made the gap concrete. Kalshi logged roughly $65 billion for the month, about 10 percent above September. Polymarket US recorded $10 billion, up about 15 percent. Among U.S.-regulated platforms Kalshi held around 83 percent, Polymarket US sat at 12 to 15 percent, and Polymarket Global fell to single digits.

The money still on the table tells the same story. Kalshi carried about $2.05 billion in open interest in October, against $384 million at Polymarket US. Across all venues DeFi Rate counted $123.4 billion traded in 30 days, with Kalshi handling 76 percent of it and $4.5 billion changing hands in the last 24 hours alone.

The drivers were not luck. Kalshi chose CFTC regulation, distribution through Robinhood and Coinbase, and breadth into sports and parlay-style contracts. Polymarket US is growing faster in percentage terms, but on a $10 billion base against $65 billion, the absolute gap is still widening heading into the midterms.

Sources: CryptoBriefing, DeFi Rate, The Block
